title: Sustained Concurrency Step-Sweep: Latency & Cost Heuristics (draft)
summary: Exploratory draft that documents a step-sweep benchmark across sustained concurrent sessions. Goal: practical heuristics for choosing parallelization and batching knobs to meet p50/p95 targets while minimizing $/token under sustained load.
body:
Purpose:
This is a working note exploring the interaction between sustained concurrency, per-session parallelism (multi-request multiplexing) and serial execution (single-threaded per-session) for the Redwood serving runtime. Focus is on practical heuristics that product and SRE can use to set defaults for Dedicated pools and autoscale thresholds.

Context and constraints:
- Workload: conversational sessions with variable turn lengths (median 80 tokens, 95th 320 tokens).
- Models: two representative configs used for the sweep: "redwood-open-7b-int8" (fast quantized) and "redwood-13b-fp16" (higher quality baseline).
- Hardware: A100-40GB and T4 as edge baseline.
- Test driver: synthetic session generator that maintains N concurrent active sessions for T windows (sustained), with random inter-turn intervals sampled from empirical distribution (mean 18s).
- Metrics captured: p50/p95 latency per token, mean throughput (tokens/s), dollars-per-1000-queries (approx using effective GPU occupancy), and KV cache hit-rate where applicable.

Experiment design:
- Step-sweep concurrency: 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200 concurrent sessions sustained for 30 minutes each.
- For each concurrency point we vary two modes: SERIAL (requests from a session processed sequentially on a single execution lane) and PARALLELIZE (session requests split across multiple lanes/strides where possible; effectively higher intra-session concurrency).
- Batching policies: small-batch (max_batch_size=8, target_latency=60ms) and dynamic-batch (batch by token-availability, target_latency=120ms).
- Observed cost is approximated by GPU-time * spot-cost; results normalized to dollars per 1k queries for comparison.

Key takeaways (provisional):
1) Low concurrency (<=25): SERIAL wins for p50 and cost on quantized model. PARALLELIZE adds scheduling overhead that hurts p50 and increases $/query by ~6-12%.
2) Mid concurrency (25-100): PARALLELIZE begins to show advantage at p95 under A100. Improved tail behavior due to better utilization and shorter queueing for large-turn sessions; cost crossover depends on batching policy.
3) High concurrency (>=100): PARALLELIZE materially reduces p95 (up to 30%) and lowers $/query when combined with dynamic batching, because higher utilization amortizes kernel setup and reduces idle GPU cycles.
4) Edge hardware (T4) is more sensitive: parallelism overheads can dominate for 13b model and for small-batch modes cause cost regressions.

Representative numbers (redwood-open-7b-int8 on A100, mid-batch policy = dynamic-batch):
- Concurrency 5: SERIAL p50=38ms, p95=72ms, $/1k=0.42
- Concurrency 25: SERIAL p50=44ms, p95=98ms, $/1k=0.39; PARALLELIZE p50=52ms, p95=88ms, $/1k=0.41
- Concurrency 100: SERIAL p50=75ms, p95=240ms, $/1k=0.58; PARALLELIZE p50=68ms, p95=168ms, $/1k=0.50
- Concurrency 200: SERIAL p50=120ms, p95=520ms, $/1k=0.90; PARALLELIZE p50=96ms, p95=360ms, $/1k=0.62

Tradeoff heuristic (draft):
- For Dedicated pools targeting p95 <= 200ms with mixed turn sizes, enable PARALLELIZE when sustained concurrency >= 75 on A100-family hardware.
- For T4 or smaller, prefer SERIAL up to concurrency 40; above that consider burst-only parallelization (enable parallelize for sessions with length > 200 tokens).
- Default autoscale policy: set target_per_gpu_sustained_sessions = 80 for A100/RTX-6000 equivalent; this keeps SERIAL within acceptable tails and pushes parallelize activation to a minority of sessions.

Text charts (ASCII) — utilization vs concurrency (approx):
Concurrency: 5   25   50   100   200
Utilization (SERIAL): 12%  45%  66%   88%   97%
Utilization (PARALLELIZE): 18%  58%  78%   95%   99%

p95 latency (ms) trend (redwood-open-7b-int8, A100):
Concurrency -> 5: 72 | 25: 98 | 50: 168 | 100: 240 | 200: 520 (SERIAL)
Concurrency -> 5: 80 | 25: 88  | 50: 120 | 100: 168 | 200: 360 (PARALLELIZE)

Cost per 1k queries (normalized dollars):
Mode/Concurrency: 5   25   50   100   200
SERIAL:            0.42 0.39 0.46 0.58 0.90
PARALLELIZE:       0.46 0.41 0.44 0.50 0.62

Operational notes and open questions:
- KV cache hit-rate interplay: sessions that achieve >30% cache hit strongly favor SERIAL because KV access is cheap relative to scheduling overhead. Need follow-up sweep isolating cache-hot vs cache-cold cohorts.
- Tail correlation with turn-size: large-turn sessions cause spikes in SERIAL because they occupy long-running lanes; consider dynamic preemption of long-running execution to reduce tail exposure.
- Billing signal: when parallelize is enabled for a session, attribute extra GPU-hours to that session's tenant to avoid hidden cross-tenant cost inflation. Design decision pending with billing/product.
- Autoscale hysteresis: observed flapping when concurrency hovered around 75–90; recommend 15% upper hysteresis window on scale-up and 25% lower on scale-down.

Next steps (short):
1) Run dedicated cache-hot vs cache-cold sweep (15m sustained windows) at conc 50/100 on both model flavors.
2) Test preemptive short-slotting: allow preemption of lanes exceeding X token output to prevent tail hogging. Measure effect on p95 and fairness.
3) Prototype cost attribution tag for parallelized sessions in telemetry (so finance can reconcile unit economics).

Appendix — quick methodology notes:
- All reported latencies are end-to-end server observable p-values (includes scheduling, batching, kernel exec).
- Cost model is conservative: uses GPU wall-time * spot-rate, excludes infra overhead and amortized control plane overhead (so actual $/1k will be higher for hosted offering).
- Synthetic driver seeded with real session length distribution from May–Dec 2027 production trace (anonymized).

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally lightweight: aim is to capture operational heuristics, not publish final numbers. When we convert to a customer-facing one-pager we will: normalize costs to Redwood-hosted rate-card, add clear versioned model tags, and include reproducible notebook link.
